source_text: Adeo satis idoneus patientiae sequester deus: si iniuriam deposueris penes eum, ultor est; si damnum, restitutor est; si dolorem, medicus est; si mortem, resuscitator est quantum patientiae licet, ut deum habeat debitorem! nec inmerito [enim. omnia enim placita eius tuetur, omnibus mandatis eius interuenit: fidem munit, pacem gubernat, dilectionem ådiuuat, humilitatem instruit, paenitentiam expectat, exhomolo. gesin adsignat, carnem regit, spiritum seruat, linguam frenat, manum continet, temptationes inculcat, scandala pellit, martyria consummat, pauperem consolatur, diuitem temperat, infirmum non consumit, ualentem non extendit, fidelem delectat. gentilem inuitat, seruum domino, dominum deo commendat. feminam exornat. uirum adprobat; amatur in puero, laudatur in iuuene, suspicitur in sene; in omni sexu, in omni aetate, formosa est. age iam, sis. et effigiem habitumque eius comprehendamus. uultus illi tranquillus et placidus, frons pura, nulla maeroris aut irae rugositate contracta; remissa aeque is laetum modum supercilia, oculis humilitate, non infelicitate deiectis; os taciturnitatis honore signatum; color, qualis securis et innoxiis; motus frequens capitis in diabolum et minax risus; ceterum amictus circum pectora candidus et corpori impressus, ut qui nec inflatur nec inquinatur. sedet! enim in throno spiritus eius mitissimi et mansuetissimi, qui non turbine glomeratur, non nubilo liuet, sed est tenerae serenitatis, apertus et simplex, quem tertio uidit Helias. nam ubi deus, ibidem et alumna eius, patientia scilicet. cum ergo spiritus dei descendit, indiuidua patientia comitatur eum. si non cum spiritu admiserimus, in nobis morabitur semper? immo nescio, an diutius perseueret- BKM sua comite ac ministra omni loco ae tempore angatur necesse est. quodcumque inimicus eius inflixerit, solus sustinere non poterit, carens instrumento sustinendi.
thought_title: Patience as God's agent and its beautiful form
orientation: Tertullian has just shown Job as the supreme example of patience and now turns to describe how patience makes God a debtor to the patient person and what patience itself looks like.
pass_a_gloss: So God is a sufficiently suitable trustee of patience: if you have deposited a wrong with him, he is an avenger; if a loss, he is a restorer; if pain, he is a physician; if death, he is a raiser-up. How much is permitted to patience, that it may have God as a debtor! And not without reason. For it guards all things pleasing to him, it intervenes in all his commands: it fortifies faith, governs peace, helps love, instructs humility, waits for repentance, assigns confession, rules the flesh, preserves the spirit, bridles the tongue, restrains the hand, tramples temptations, drives away stumbling blocks, consummates martyrdoms, consoles the poor, tempers the rich, does not consume the weak, does not stretch out the strong, delights the faithful. It invites the pagan, commends the slave to the master, the master to God. It adorns the woman, proves the man; it is loved in the boy, praised in the young man, looked up to in the old man; in every sex, in every age, it is beautiful. Come now, if you please, let us also grasp its appearance and its dress. Its face is calm and gentle, its brow pure, contracted by no wrinkling of grief or anger; its eyebrows relaxed equally into a joyful measure, its eyes cast down with humility, not with unhappiness; its mouth sealed with the honor of silence; its color such as belongs to the carefree and the harmless; frequent movement of its head against the devil and a threatening laugh; for the rest, its clothing around the breast is white and pressed to the body, as one that is neither puffed up nor defiled. For it sits on the throne of its most gentle and most mild spirit, which is not whirled up by a whirlwind, is not black with a cloud, but is of tender serenity, open and simple, which Elijah saw third. For where God is, there also is his foster child, patience, of course. Therefore when the Spirit of God descends, indivisible patience accompanies him. If we have not admitted it with the Spirit, will it remain in us always? Rather I do not know whether it will continue longer. Without its companion and minister it must be distressed in every place and time. Whatever its enemy inflicts, it will not be able to endure alone, lacking the instrument of enduring.

choices.why: The term denotes a neutral depositary to whom something is entrusted for safekeeping; 'trustee' captures the legal and custodial sense without implying a financial institution.
The glossary bans 'punishment' and 'retaliation' for ultio; 'avenger' preserves the active agent sense of ultor while staying within the revenge semantic field.
A literal rendering of the agent noun from resuscito, preserving the parallel structure with 'avenger', 'restorer', 'physician'.
Alumna means a nursling or foster child, emphasizing the intimate nurturing relationship between God and patience; 'foster child' keeps the familial image.
Inculco literally means to tread or stamp upon; 'tramples' conveys the forceful overcoming of temptations.
The phrase describes patience's mocking defiance of the devil; 'threatening laugh' preserves both the menace and the derision.

bible_refs.note: quem tertio uidit Helias — Elijah's encounter with the still small voice after wind, earthquake, and fire

pass_b_english: So God is a fully sufficient trustee of patience. If you deposit a wrong with him, he is the avenger; if a loss, the restorer; if pain, the physician; if death, the raiser-up. How much patience is allowed, to have God as a debtor! And not without reason. For patience guards all his good pleasure, and comes between us and all his commands. It fortifies faith, governs peace, assists love, instructs humility, waits for repentance, marks out confession, rules the flesh, preserves the spirit, bridles the tongue, restrains the hand, tramples temptations, drives away scandals, consummates martyrdom, consoles the poor, tempers the rich, does not crush the weak, does not stretch the strong, delights the faithful, invites the pagan, commends the servant to his master and the master to God, adorns the woman, approves the man. It is loved in the boy, praised in the young man, looked up to in the old man. In every sex, in every age, it is beautiful.

Come now, let us also grasp its appearance and bearing. Its face is tranquil and calm, its brow pure, contracted by no wrinkle of sorrow or anger. Its eyebrows are relaxed in a measured way, its eyes cast down with humility, not with misery. Its mouth is sealed with the honor of silence. Its color is that of the carefree and innocent. Its head moves often toward the devil with a threatening laugh. For the rest, its clothing is white, pressed close around the chest and body, as of one who is neither puffed up nor defiled. For it sits on the throne of that most gentle and mild spirit, who is not whirled up in a storm, nor dark with cloud, but is of tender serenity, open and simple, whom Elijah saw third (1 Kings 19:12). For where God is, there also is his foster child, patience, of course. When the Spirit of God descends, then patience accompanies him inseparably. If we do not admit it along with the Spirit, will it remain in us always? No, I do not know whether it will persist longer. Without its companion and minister, it must be distressed at every place and time. Whatever its enemy inflicts, it will not be able to endure alone, lacking the instrument of endurance.
notes: The source text contains apparent OCR damage: 'ådiuuat' for 'adiuuat', 'exhomolo. gesin' for 'exhomologesin', 'sedet! enim' for 'sedet enim', and 'BKM' which appears to be a stray abbreviation or corruption. The gloss renders the evident intended readings.

problems.quote: Its head moves often toward the devil with a threatening laugh
problems.why: Personified Patience laughing at the devil is odd and unclear in context.
problems.fix: Clarify this is allegorical defiance of temptation.

edits.old: Its head moves often toward the devil with a threatening laugh.
edits.new: It often shakes its head at the devil with a threatening laugh.

fixed: The source reads 'motus frequens capitis in diabolum et minax risus' — 'frequent movement of its head against the devil and a threatening laugh.' The English 'moves often toward the devil' misreads 'in diabolum' as motion toward the devil rather than a gesture directed against him. 'Shakes its head at the devil' captures the allegorical defiance of temptation.
